title: Type 2 Diabetes: Confirm the Diagnosis, Then Treat Risk and Glycemia
bottomLine: Diagnose type 2 diabetes using Canadian laboratory criteria and confirm an abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient. Initial management is not glucose-only: classify the diabetes, assess cardiorenal risk and complications, set an individualized target, and choose therapy based on severity, comorbidity, hypoglycemia risk, weight, kidney function, cost and patient preference.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, recurrent infection or blurred vision can accompany hyperglycemia, but many people are asymptomatic.
Severe symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketosis or catabolic weight loss should raise concern for insulin deficiency or metabolic decompensation rather than routine outpatient oral-therapy sequencing.
differentiate: Type 1/LADA, steroid-induced diabetes, pancreatic disease and other secondary causes can mimic type 2 diabetes.
A1C can be misleading with altered red-cell turnover, selected hemoglobinopathies, advanced kidney/liver disease and other conditions.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, family history, medication contributors, pregnancy, BP, smoking, ASCVD, HF, CKD, albuminuria, hypoglycemia risk and social access to nutrition/medication.
workup: Use FPG, A1C, OGTT or random plasma glucose according to Canadian criteria and symptoms; confirm asymptomatic abnormal testing appropriately.
Establish renal function, urine albumin, lipids and complication screening based on current diabetes guidance.
management: Use healthy-behaviour support plus pharmacotherapy individualized to A1C/severity and comorbidity.
Metformin remains appropriate for many people, but cardiorenal indications can justify SGLT2 inhibitor/GLP-1RA use independent of A1C target.
Use insulin promptly for metabolic decompensation or severe symptomatic hyperglycemia.
medicationSafety: Renal function, pregnancy, hypoglycemia risk and acute illness alter medication choice.
SGLT2 inhibitors require euglycemic-DKA/sick-day/perioperative counselling; insulin and sulfonylureas carry higher hypoglycemia risk.
redFlags: Marked dehydration or altered mental status
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing language and explain why heart/kidney protection can matter even when glucose looks acceptable.
Set a concrete follow-up plan after diagnosis rather than giving lifestyle advice alone.
followUp: Reassess glycemia, tolerability, renal function and complications after treatment changes.
examTrap: Calling every adult with hyperglycemia type 2 diabetes and delaying insulin despite ketosis or catabolic symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Confirm the diagnosis, classify the diabetes, then treat the whole cardiovascular-renal risk profile.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada diagnosis and 2024 pharmacologic-management guidance

title: Diabetes Medication Selection Beyond Metformin: Match the Drug to the Patient
bottomLine: After or alongside metformin, drug selection is driven by ASCVD, HF, CKD, albuminuria, weight goals, hypoglycemia risk, renal function, adverse effects, access and preference. Do not rank agents by A1C lowering alone when cardiorenal outcome benefit changes the decision.
recognize: SGLT2 inhibitors and selected GLP-1 receptor agonists can provide cardiovascular/renal benefit beyond glucose lowering in appropriate patients.
Sulfonylureas and insulin are effective but have more hypoglycemia risk, especially with CKD, frailty or irregular meals.
differentiate: DPP-4 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists are generally not combined for routine glycemic benefit.
A drug appropriate for obesity/ASCVD may be wrong for severe gastroparesis, recurrent genital infection, advanced renal disease or affordability constraints.
assessment: Set an individualized A1C goal and assess ASCVD, HF, CKD/eGFR/albuminuria, weight, hypoglycemia history, pregnancy, medication coverage and adherence barriers.
workup: Use renal function and cause-specific baseline monitoring before selecting agents; A1C alone is insufficient when it is unreliable or when cardiorenal indications dominate.
management: Choose therapy for both glycemic and organ-protection goals.
Use combination therapy when A1C is substantially above target or when compelling indications support it.
De-intensify when treatment burden/hypoglycemia outweighs benefit.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors: volume depletion, genital infection and euglycemic DKA risk; hold in major fasting/acute illness/perioperative settings per current guidance.
GLP-1 therapies: GI effects, dehydration and gallbladder/pancreatitis warning symptoms; product-specific contraindications apply.
Sulfonylureas/insulin: hypoglycemia risk increases with CKD/frailty.
redFlags: Euglycemic DKA symptoms on SGLT2 therapy
counselling: Explain why medication choice may target heart/kidney risk even when A1C is at goal.
Review sick-day rules and medication-specific red flags.
followUp: Track A1C/glucose, weight, renal function, adverse effects and outcome-specific goals.
examTrap: Refusing an organ-protective medication because the A1C is already controlled.
oneLinePearl: Beyond metformin, choose for the heart, kidneys, weight and hypoglycemia risk—not only the A1C.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2024 pharmacologic glycemic management update

title: DKA: Ketones and Acidosis, Not Just Hyperglycemia
bottomLine: DKA is a ketosis/acidosis emergency caused by insulin deficiency. Treat in parallel: restore volume, assess/replace potassium, give insulin safely, monitor acid-base/ketone resolution and identify the trigger. DKA can occur with only modest glucose, especially with SGLT2 inhibitor exposure or pregnancy.
recognize: Vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, tachypnea/Kussmaul breathing and altered mental status are common.
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is more informative than urine ketones when available.
differentiate: HHS has more profound hyperosmolality/dehydration and less prominent ketoacidosis but mixed presentations occur.
Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can mimic portions of the biochemical pattern.
assessment: Assess ABCs, perfusion, mental status, volume status, infection/ischemia, insulin access/adherence, pregnancy and SGLT2 use.
Obtain ECG when significant potassium abnormality is possible.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, venous/arterial acid-base testing as appropriate, beta-hydroxybutyrate/ketones and anion gap.
Investigate precipitant with cause-directed cultures, ECG/troponin or imaging.
management: Use protocolized isotonic fluids, potassium-guided insulin and dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketosis.
Do not start insulin blindly in severe hypokalemia.
Continue treatment until ketoacidosis resolves clinically/biochemically, not merely until glucose normalizes.
medicationSafety: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can cause dangerous hypokalemia.
SGLT2-associated DKA can be euglycemic; normal-ish glucose does not exclude the diagnosis.
counselling: After recovery, teach sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin continuity and SGLT2 hold situations when applicable.
followUp: Address the precipitant and access/adherence barriers before discharge.
examTrap: Stopping insulin once glucose normalizes while ketosis/acidosis persists.
oneLinePearl: DKA ends when the ketoacidosis resolves, not when the glucose looks better.

title: Hypoglycemia: Treat the Low, Then Prevent the Next One
bottomLine: Correct hypoglycemia immediately, then identify why it happened. Recurrent or severe hypoglycemia is a medication-safety event and should trigger regimen redesign, assessment of renal function/food access/hypoglycemia awareness and prevention planning—not repeated rescue treatment alone.
recognize: Adrenergic symptoms include tremor, sweating, palpitations and hunger; neuroglycopenia causes confusion, behaviour change, seizure or coma.
Older adults may present with falls/delirium rather than classic symptoms.
differentiate: Conscious patients who can swallow use oral fast carbohydrate; severe episodes require glucagon or IV glucose according to setting.
Sulfonylurea or long-acting-insulin hypoglycemia can recur after initial correction.
assessment: Check glucose promptly and assess airway/neurologic status/injury.
Review insulin/secretagogue doses, missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal/hepatic disease, illness and food insecurity.
workup: Persistent unexplained hypoglycemia without glucose-lowering therapy requires a dedicated diagnostic evaluation rather than assuming poor intake.
management: For mild episodes, use Diabetes Canada fast-carbohydrate treatment and recheck timing.
For severe episodes, use glucagon/IV glucose and emergency support as appropriate.
Modify the causative regimen, targets or monitoring plan after recovery.
medicationSafety: CKD and frailty amplify insulin/secretagogue risk; glyburide is particularly problematic in older adults/renal impairment.
Recurrent hypoglycemia should prompt de-intensification rather than advice to simply eat more.
counselling: Teach carrying fast carbohydrate, glucagon use, driving precautions and recognition of impaired awareness.
followUp: Review CGM/SMBG patterns and medication changes after any severe event.
examTrap: Treating the glucose successfully and sending the patient home on the unchanged causative regimen.
oneLinePearl: Fix the glucose, then fix the reason it fell.

title: Hypothyroidism: Diagnose the Axis Before Adjusting Levothyroxine
bottomLine: Primary hypothyroidism is usually high TSH with low free T4; central hypothyroidism can have low free T4 with inappropriately normal/low TSH. Dose levothyroxine to the correct axis and clinical context, and check adherence/administration/interactions before escalating from one abnormal TSH.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, menstrual change and bradycardia are common but nonspecific.
Older adults may have subtle symptoms; pregnancy increases hormone requirements and target urgency.
differentiate: Central hypothyroidism requires free T4 interpretation and pituitary/adrenal evaluation rather than TSH titration alone.
Non-thyroidal illness and assay interference can distort thyroid tests.
assessment: Review symptoms, pregnancy, cardiac disease, pituitary symptoms, adherence, timing with food/calcium/iron and interacting medications.
workup: Use TSH first for most primary disease and add free T4 when abnormal or central disease suspected.
Do not repeat antibodies serially to titrate replacement.
management: Use levothyroxine replacement individualized to age, cardiac disease and severity; titrate after sufficient time to reach steady state.
Pregnancy requires prompt dose/monitoring adjustment.
medicationSafety: Overreplacement increases atrial fibrillation and bone risk; underreplacement can persist if absorption/adherence issues are not corrected.
If central adrenal insufficiency is possible, address cortisol deficiency before thyroid replacement.
counselling: Teach consistent dosing and separation from interfering supplements/medications.
followUp: Recheck thyroid function after meaningful dose changes and more frequently in pregnancy.
examTrap: Increasing levothyroxine from one high TSH without asking how the medication is taken.
oneLinePearl: Before changing the dose, verify the axis, the timing, and the adherence.

title: Hyperthyroidism: Confirm Thyrotoxicosis, Then Find the Cause
bottomLine: Thyrotoxicosis is the biochemical/clinical state; treatment depends on the cause. Confirm suppressed TSH with free thyroid hormone testing, distinguish Graves/toxic nodules from thyroiditis or exogenous hormone, control symptoms safely, and recognize thyroid storm as an acute-care emergency.
recognize: Weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance, palpitations, frequent stool and proximal weakness are common; older adults may present with AF or apathy.
Graves can include diffuse goitre and eye disease.
differentiate: Thyroiditis releases stored hormone and does not respond to antithyroid medication like Graves/toxic nodules.
Biotin/assay interference or exogenous hormone can mimic endogenous disease.
assessment: Assess HR/rhythm, heart failure, eye symptoms, goitre/nodules, pregnancy, iodine/amiodarone exposure and precipitating illness.
workup: Use TSH plus free T4/T3 as appropriate and etiology-directed antibodies or imaging when needed.
management: Control adrenergic symptoms when appropriate and use antithyroid drugs/radioiodine/surgery according to cause, pregnancy and patient factors.
Thyroid storm requires emergency multidrug treatment and trigger management.
medicationSafety: Fever/sore throat on antithyroid medication requires urgent agranulocytosis assessment; hepatic injury symptoms require prompt evaluation.
Pregnancy changes drug selection and timing.
counselling: Teach antithyroid drug red flags and smoking cessation for thyroid eye disease.
followUp: Trend thyroid function and definitive-treatment planning by etiology.
examTrap: Escalating antithyroid medication in thyroiditis without establishing the cause of thyrotoxicosis.
oneLinePearl: Treat thyrotoxicosis by cause—not by the suppressed TSH alone.

title: Thyroid Nodule: TSH and Ultrasound Risk Before FNA
bottomLine: A thyroid nodule is evaluated with TSH plus risk-based ultrasound assessment. FNA depends on sonographic risk and size, not palpability or patient anxiety alone; a suppressed TSH changes the pathway toward functional-nodule evaluation.
recognize: Rapid growth, hard/fixed nodule, cervical adenopathy, hoarseness, radiation exposure and strong family history are concerning.
Most thyroid nodules are benign and many do not require biopsy.
differentiate: A suppressed TSH suggests autonomous function and changes the workup.
Diffuse thyroid enlargement without a discrete nodule follows a different pathway.
assessment: Assess compressive symptoms, voice change, thyroid symptoms, radiation/family history and cervical nodes.
workup: Order TSH and thyroid ultrasound; use accepted sonographic risk/size criteria to determine FNA.
Avoid routine broad thyroid testing or biopsy of every incidental nodule.
management: Refer suspicious cytology/nodes or compressive disease and surveil lower-risk nodules at evidence-based intervals.
Manage hyperfunctioning nodules according to thyroid status and specialty pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not use routine levothyroxine suppression for benign nodules because harms can exceed benefit.
counselling: Explain why many nodules are monitored rather than biopsied immediately.
followUp: Repeat ultrasound only at intervals justified by sonographic risk and prior results.
examTrap: Biopsying every thyroid nodule regardless of ultrasound risk and size.
oneLinePearl: Thyroid nodule FNA is ultrasound-risk driven, not fear driven.

title: Adrenal Insufficiency: Chronic Replacement, Acute Crisis Recognition
bottomLine: Adrenal insufficiency can be primary or central and presents with nonspecific fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and electrolyte/glucose abnormalities. In a stable patient, confirm the axis with appropriate cortisol/ACTH testing; in suspected adrenal crisis, give stress-dose glucocorticoid and fluids immediately and do not wait for confirmatory results.
recognize: Primary adrenal insufficiency can cause hyperpigmentation, salt craving, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia; central disease usually preserves mineralocorticoid function.
Crisis presents with hypotension/shock, vomiting/abdominal pain, severe weakness, hypoglycemia and electrolyte disturbance.
differentiate: Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid exposure can suppress the HPA axis and create central adrenal insufficiency.
Sepsis/GI illness can mimic crisis but may also precipitate it.
assessment: Review steroid exposure, autoimmune disease, pituitary disease, weight loss, GI symptoms, orthostasis, hyperpigmentation and pregnancy.
In instability, assess perfusion, glucose/electrolytes and precipitating infection/illness.
workup: Use morning cortisol/ACTH and dynamic testing as indicated in stable patients; renin/aldosterone support primary disease assessment.
Draw cortisol/ACTH before emergency steroids only if this does not delay treatment.
management: Use physiologic glucocorticoid replacement and mineralocorticoid replacement for confirmed primary deficiency when indicated.
Adrenal crisis requires immediate parenteral glucocorticoid, isotonic fluids and precipitant treatment.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly stop prolonged systemic glucocorticoids when HPA suppression is plausible.
Stress dosing is glucocorticoid management; increasing fludrocortisone alone does not treat adrenal crisis.
redFlags: Persistent vomiting/inability to retain oral steroid
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, emergency injection, medical alert identification and when to seek emergency care.
followUp: Review replacement adequacy, BP/electrolytes and recurrent-crisis prevention.
examTrap: Waiting for ACTH stimulation testing before treating a hypotensive patient with known adrenal insufficiency and vomiting.
oneLinePearl: Diagnose carefully when stable; treat first when crisis is plausible.
sourceBasis: Endocrine Society adrenal-insufficiency guidance used where Canadian specialty guidance is silent
